transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Linda Kenyon.
Tennessee's prison chief has submitted his resignation
following the botched execution of Christa Pike,
which her attorneys say left her unconscious and on a ventilator.
NPR's Frank Langford reports.
In a statement, Frank Strada, the commissioner of the Tennessee Department of Prisons,
said his resignation was in the state's best interest
as it launches an independent review of what went wrong.
"I believe this review is entirely appropriate and necessary,
as I look forward to doing everything I can
to help determine exactly what occurred," the statement read.
Tennessee officials failed to execute Pike Wednesday
after administering two doses of pentobarbital.
Witnesses said after Pike received the first dose,
she said her arm was burning.
Pike, then 18, was convicted of killing a classmate in 1995.
This was the second failed execution in Tennessee this year.
Executioners tried for over an hour to place an IV into a man
convicted of kidnapping and killing three people in 1994.
Frank Langford, NPR News.
Americans could see some relief from high fuel prices
after the G7 nations agreed to release
100 million barrels of oil and fuel from emergency reserves.
But as NPR's Windsor Johnston reports, that relief may be short-lived.
Americans could see diesel prices start to ease this month
as emergency fuel reserves reach the market.
Tom Closa, chief energy advisor for Gulf Oil, says any relief
will be temporary, warning that the cost of diesel
will keep the pressure on household budgets.
"That's going to infiltrate every nook and cranny of the economy,
whether it be groceries.
Remember, the farmers have to pay these prices for diesel
in its harvest season, or whether it be items
that you might buy for Christmas.
Instead of being shipped for $10, it's going to be $12."
Closa says the bigger test will come this winter,
especially for households in the Northeast that rely on heating oil.
Windsor Johnston, NPR News.
President Trump's proposed triumphal arch is getting closer to final approval,
despite public opposition and an ongoing lawsuit.
NPR's Rachel Treisman reports.
A federal panel packed with Trump allies abruptly canceled
the historic preservation review process for his proposed arch last month,
sidestepping one of the last remaining hurdles.
Concerned citizens this week joined veterans
and Democratic lawmakers in Memorial Circle to speak out against it.
John Gunderson is one of the Vietnam War veterans
and retired foreign service members
that has sued the government to block the arch,
which would tower over Arlington National Cemetery.
"I hope people look at this. They look at it in a logical, nonpartisan way.
It's a waste of taxpayers' money. Stop the arch."
Even if the arch does proceed,
Democrats at the protest said they would fight to knock it down.
Rachel Treisman, NPR News.
You're listening to NPR.
Protests continue across Spain,
as residents there demand the government take urgent action
to address a national housing crisis.
NPR's Miguel Macias has the story.
Much has happened since the protests started a week ago.
After 87-year-old Maria del Carmen Abascal was evicted
from her rental apartment in Madrid,
the government of Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez
drafted two emergency housing decrees in a rush,
negotiating with these coalition members.
While all parties in Spain agree there is a national problem
with the price of rental housing,
they did not agree on a solution.
On Friday, Sanchez's measures were voted down.
In Congress, there's been plenty of finger-pointing
and speculation that Sanchez might call snap elections for late November,
as he sees an opportunity to come from behind in the polls
thanks to an energized left.
On the streets, protesters continue to demand solutions now.
Miguel Macias, NPR News, Seville, Spain.
A Tokyo court has awarded legal protection to a human instead of AI.
The case involves a popular Japanese anime voice actor,
whose voice was used without permission, on TikTok.
The decision marks the first time Japan has acknowledged voice rights.
Kanjiro Suda had sued over an AI clone of his voice
that was used in the TikTok videos.
The ruling in his favor comes as concerns rise
among voice actors about AI cloning.
The TikTok accounting question has already been closed.
I'm Lyndi Kenyon, NPR News, in Washington.
This message comes from EasyCater, the workplace food platform.
EasyCater helps organizations order food from favorite restaurants,
meet dietary needs, and stay on budget,
with employee meal programs, flexible payment options,

Learn more at EasyCater.com.

topics.text: Tennessee prison chief Frank Strada resigns following botched execution of Christa Pike
G7 nations agree to release 100 million barrels of oil from emergency reserves
Trump's proposed triumphal arch over Arlington National Cemetery moves closer to approval
Spanish residents protest national housing crisis after government housing decrees voted down
Tokyo court awards legal protection to voice actor Kanjiro Suda over AI clone
